title: Here Comes Santa Claude
text:
When Cynthia Bell McGillis needs help with her holiday shopping, she turns to Mrs. Claus. Not the one in the North Pole, but her own custom-built AI agent. After getting a head start on buying Christmas presents last month, McGillis had an idea of how to more easily keep track of her purchases: “I bet Grok can help with that,” McGillis, who works in marketing for an AI start-up in San Diego, told me. She instructed Grok Bot, an AI assistant made by Elon Musk, to constantly scan her email inbox every day. “Mrs. Claus” now logs arriving items and who they are for, searches the newsletters McGillis subscribes to for sales on potential gift ideas, and keeps a running total of how much McGillis has spent. The day we spoke, the bot had just surfaced a discount on Old Navy Christmas-themed pajamas.

 In recent months, tech companies have launched a number of AI personal assistants, one after the other. Instinct, an agent that allows users to chat with it directly from the iMessage app, went viral in August ; the next month, Meta launched its competitor, Muse. According to Mark Zuckerberg, more than 10 million users tried Muse in its first six weeks. Unlike traditional chatbots, AI agents can act on your behalf in the real world: Feed them your credit-card information and online passwords (if you dare), and they can find restaurant reservations, book flights, and, yes, buy gifts on your behalf. This month, OpenAI debuted ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its agents to also make purchases for users.

 [ Read: AI agents are here. Nobody’s ready. ] 

 Now, for the first time, some people are about to open presents that were chosen and purchased entirely by bots. When Rohit Bakshi, an AI-product director in the Bay Area, wanted to get his nephew a Tin Can, the popular Wi-Fi-enabled “landline” for kids , he messaged Instinct to buy it. Bakshi told me that using Instinct more for holiday shopping would be a “no-brainer.” I heard similar enthusiasm from Boaz Sobrado, a tech worker also based in the Bay Area. (Every agentic-AI-loving shopper I could find had some connection to the tech industry.) Sobrado recently asked his girlfriend’s Muse agent, which knows her Instagram likes and saved posts, to find a hotel that matched her tastes. Agents can crawl through hundreds of text messages and emails to identify a tailored gift—something the intended recipient mentioned a long time ago, maybe, or something they might like based on contextual clues.

 AI companies are certainly invested in the notion that their personal assistants can be heroes this holiday season. In an email, Ben Schwerin, the chief business officer of Instinct, told me that the company has seen a recent uptick in people using its agents to shop. “What’s been interesting is people are trusting Instinct to complete purchases for a full gift list, rather than handing Instinct one-off links,” he said. Meanwhile, Meta is partnering with social-media influencers to tout how Muse can be used for holiday shopping, such as by choosing gifts on a budget. (Meta declined to answer questions about how people are using Muse for holiday shopping.)

 Americans without ties to the tech industry so far seem less bought in. AI assistants, for the most part, have yet to fully enter the mainstream. Some of that gap may be principled: Much of the country, after all, remains concerned about AI’s rapid development, and people certainly have good reason to be uncomfortable with the idea of a bot shopping with their credit card and having detailed access to their family’s personal information. AI assistants can also be expensive, many requiring subscriptions that run more than $100 a month. Some major retailers, including Amazon, have banned AI agents; the e-commerce giant is reportedly worried about what shopping bots could mean for its advertising business.

 Still, it may be only a matter of time. The promise of convenience can be hard to ignore. Lots of people who aren’t using agents to shop on their behalf are still asking AI for gift-giving help. This year, 40 percent of shoppers say they plan to use generative AI for holiday shopping, such as by asking ChatGPT for product recommendations, according to a recent report from Accenture. Kath Gramling, who leads the consumer-goods-and-retail division at Accenture, believes that many people who use LLMs may soon adopt AI agents too. “It’s just a natural extension,” Gramling told me.

 More shoppers may soon experience what can go wrong when you let an AI personal assistant run wild. One man claimed on X that his AI agent accidentally posted his bank-account balances in a Slack channel at his workplace; another man told Business Insider that a request for ingredients to make dinner for two resulted in a 20-pound chicken-wing order. Indeed, not all of Sobrado’s purchases have been successful: He recently ordered flowers for his girlfriend using his Muse agent, which he named Hermenegildo. When the flowers arrived, he realized that the agent had attached a card for his girlfriend and signed it, With love, Hermenegildo .

 [ Read: It’s all fun and games until you give AI your credit card ] 

 Even if you aren’t using an AI personal assistant to buy any gifts, the bots might still affect your holiday-shopping experience. Last month, a Verge reporter wrote that she was able to instruct her Muse agent to continuously hold items in her cart on the RealReal, blocking other potential shoppers from purchasing them on the secondhand-luxury-fashion website. (Following the report, the RealReal said that the company would make it more difficult for agents to shop on its website.) And yesterday, Walmart announced that the company will now let Muse agents browse for deals and make purchases on users’ behalf. Black Fridays of decades past were an endurance game of who could wake up at the crack of dawn and brave the freezing weather in pursuit of a deal. This Black Friday might be a competition of who has the best AI agent.

 All of this raises the age-old holiday question: What is gift giving really for ? AI agents will never be able to replicate the experiential aspects of holiday magic. I love spending weeks clicking through websites until I feel the eureka moment of finding the perfect gift that I know someone will love. Others enjoy walking in a physical mall during the holidays, past the twinkling lights and smiling Santa. Bakshi told me that he can’t imagine letting Instinct do all of his holiday shopping. “I like going to the stores,” he said. “There’s a lot of festivity to it.”

 The principle stands that a Christmas gift is supposed to symbolize the love and appreciation you feel for a recipient. Instead, gift-giving frequently becomes a matter of commercialism and obligation. Now AI agents are opening the possibility of delivering incredibly personal gifts with about the same effort it takes to purchase a gift card. Hopefully for gift givers, they’ll get everyone’s name right.
